title: Check yourself: when parallel streams pay

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: What does this page expect when a sum over a five-element list is moved to a parallel stream?

options.text: It runs about five times faster, one core taking each of the five numbers
options.says: The page says the benefit is not guaranteed and that splitting and coordination cost more than they save on small data.

options.text: It runs slower, since splitting and merging cost more than the work they share
options.says: The page says the overhead of splitting, coordination and combining exceeds the benefit for small datasets.

options.text: It runs at the same speed, since the JVM quietly keeps small pipelines on one thread
options.says: The page describes no such switch; it says the parallel overhead itself dominates for small datasets.

questions.stem: What does this page say about a parallel stream whose map step waits on database calls?

options.text: Its results get corrupted, since each thread's list is unsafe to merge
options.says: The page says collect with toList, toSet or groupingBy is safe because each thread accumulates into its own container.

options.text: It is the best fit, since I/O-heavy work is where this feature does best
options.says: The page says the feature shines for CPU-bound work on large datasets, and to avoid I/O in it.

options.text: Its blocked threads starve other tasks that share the common pool
options.says: The page says blocking in ForkJoinPool threads starves other tasks, and suggests virtual threads or async I/O instead.

concepts: Blocking I/O inside a parallel stream ties up the shared common pool's threads.
Parallelism has a cost in splitting and merging, so it loses on small data and pays only on large CPU-bound work.
